Q: What does the "as const" mean in TypeScript and what is its use case? A: 
Traditionally in JavaScript, we have a config object and use Object.freeze to make it immutable. However, this only works at the first level (not for nested objects). It is executed at runtime and errors appear in production.

as const in TypeScript works for nested levels as well and shows errors while writing the code, since TypeScript is a development tool.

Using TypeScript, we faces a lot error in runtime (production) issues.


Object.freeze makes an object immutable at runtime, while as const makes it immutable and more specific at compile-time (TypeScript types).

Q: Java: How to read a text file A:

tl;dr

Use the features of modern Java.

    Arrays
            .stream(
                    Files
                            .readString(   // Automatically opens & closes the file. Defaults to UTF-8 character encoding. 
                                Paths.get( "/Users/basil_dot_work/integers.txt" ) 
                            )              // Returns a `String` object containing all the text in the file. 
                            .trim()        // Remove newlines & whitespace.
                            .strip()       // Ditto
                            .split( " " )  // Returns an array, `String[]`. 
            )                              // Returns a stream of the elements of that `String[]` array. 
            .map( Integer :: valueOf )     // Convert each string into an `Integer` object. 
            .toList()                      // Collect all those `Integer` objects into a `List`.

Modern Java

We can use features of modern Java to simplify this work: NIO.2 (Paths & Files), Stream, method reference.

Locate the file.

Path path = Paths.get( " /path/to/integers.txt" );

Read the file into memory as a String. Defaults to UTF-8. Call strip & trim to remove any line-terminator or whitespace.

String input = Files.readString( path ).trim().strip() ;

Split the string into parts, based on SPACE character as the delimiter.

String[] parts = input.split( " " ) ;

Parse each part, each String, as an Integer. Collect into a List.

List < Integer > integers =
        Arrays
                .stream( parts )
                .map( Integer :: valueOf )
                .toList();

Dump to console.

integers.forEach( IO :: println );

Put all that code together, along with a necessary try-catch.

Path path = Paths.get( "/path/to/integers.txt" );
try
{
    String input = Files.readString( path ).trim().strip();
    String[] parts = input.split( " " );
    List < Integer > integers =
            Arrays
                    .stream( parts )
                    .map( Integer :: valueOf )
                    .toList();
    integers.forEach( IO :: println );
}
catch ( IOException e ) { throw new RuntimeException( e ); }

When run:

1
62
4
55
5
6
77

Not that I recommend it, but we could make this a one-liner.

try
{
    Arrays
            .stream(
                    Files
                            .readString(   // Automatically opens & closes the file. Defaults to UTF-8 character encoding. 
                                Paths.get( "/Users/basil_dot_work/integers.txt" ) 
                            )              // Returns a `String` object containing all the text in the file. 
                            .trim()        // Remove newlines & whitespace.
                            .strip()       // Ditto
                            .split( " " )  // Returns an array, `String[]`. 
            )                              // Returns a stream of the elements of that `String[]` array. 
            .map( Integer :: valueOf )     // Convert each string into an `Integer` object. 
            .forEach( IO :: println );     // Dump each `Integer` object to console by implicitly calling its `toString` method. 
}
catch ( IOException e )
{
    throw new RuntimeException( e );
}
